source_text: Πλούτου τοίνυν μεταληπτέον ἀξιολόγως καὶ μεταδοτέον φιλανθρώπως, οὐ βαναύσως οὐδὲ ἀλαζονικῶς, οὐδὲ ἐκτρεπτέον τὸ φιλόκαλον εἰς φιλαυτίαν καὶ ἀπειροκαλίαν, μή πῃ ἄρα καὶ πρὸς ἡμᾶς φήσῃ τις· ὁ ἵππος αὐτοῦ πεντεκαίδεκα ταλάντων ἐστὶν ἄξιος ἢ τὸ χωρίον ἢ ὁ οἰκέτης ἢ τὸ χρυσίον, αὐτὸς δὲ χαλκῶν ἐστι τίμιος τριῶν. αὐτίκα γοῦν περίελε τὸν κόσμον τῶν γυναικῶν καὶ τοὺς οἰκέτας τῶν δεσποτῶν, οὐδὲν διαφέροντας τῶν ἀργυρωνήτων εὑρήσεις. τοὺς δεσπότας, οὐκ ἐν βαδίσματι, οὐκ ἐν βλέμματι, οὐκ ἐν φθέγματι· οὕτως τοίνυν τοῖς ἀνδραπόδοις ἐοίκασιν. ἀλλὰ καὶ τῷ ἀσθενέστεροι εἶναι τῶν οἰκετῶν διακρίνονται καὶ τῷ νοσηλότερον ἀνατεθράφθαι. ἄριστον γοῦν δογμάτων τοῦτο ᾄδειν παρ᾿ ἕκαστα χρή, ὡς ὁ μὲν ἀγαθὸς ἀνὴρ σώφρων ὢν καὶ δίκαιος ἐν οὐρανῷ θησαυρίζει τὰ χρήματα· οὗτος [ὁ] τὰ ἐπίγεια καταπωλήσας καὶ πτωχοῖς ἐπιδοὺς τὸν ἀνώλεθρον ἐξευρίσκει θησαυρόν, ἔνθα οὐ σής, οὐ λῃστής· μακάριος οὗτος ὄντως, ἐάν τε σμικρὸς καὶ ἀσθενὴς καὶ ἄδοξος ᾖ, καὶ πλοῦτον ὄντως πλουτεῖ τὸν μέγιστον· ἐὰν δὲ ἄρα πλουτῇ μὲν Κινύρα τε καὶ Μίδα μᾶλλον, ᾖ δὲ ἄδικος καὶ ὑφερήφανος, καθάπερ ὁ ἐν τῇ πορφύρᾳ καὶ βύσσῳ τρυφῶν καὶ τὸν Λάζαρον ὑπερηφανῶν, ἄθλιός τέ ἐστι καὶ ἀνιαρῶς ζῇ καὶ οὐ ζήσεται. ἐοικέναι γοῦν μοι δοκεῖ ὁ πλοῦτος ἑρπετῷ, οὗ εἰ μή τις ἐπίσταιτο λαβέσθαι ἀβλαβῶς, πόρρωθεν ἀκινδύνως ἄκρας οὐρᾶς ἀνακρημνὰς τὸ θηρίον, περιπλέξεται τῇ χειρὶ καὶ δήξεται· δεινὸς δὲ καὶ ὁ πλοῦτος ἰλυσπώμενος παρὰ τὴν ἔμπειρον ἢ ἄπειρον αὐτοῦ λαβὴν προσφῦναι καὶ δάκνειν, εἰ μή τις αὐτῷ καταμεγαλοφρονῶν ἐπιστημόνως χρῷτο, ἵνα σὺν τῇ ἐπῳδῇ τοῦ λόγου καταξέσηται μὲν τὸ θηρίον, αὐτὸς δὲ ἀπαθὴς μείνῃ. ἀλλ᾿, ὡς ἔοικεν, τὰ πλείονος ἄξια κεκτημένος πλούσιος ὢν μόνος ἐλελήθει· πολλοῦ δὲ ἄξια οὐ λίθος, οὐκ ἄργυρος, οὐκ ἐσθής, οὐ κάλλος σώματος, ἀλλ᾿ ἡ ἀρετή, ὅς ἐστι λόγος διὰ τοῦ παιδαγωγοῦ παραδιδόμενος εἰς ἄσκησιν· λόγος οὗτος ὁ τὴν τρυφὴν ἐξομνύμενος, τὴν δὲ αὐτουργίαν διάκονον παρακαλῶν καὶ τὴν εὐτέλειαν ἐξυμνῶν τῆς σωφροσύνης τὴν ἔγγονον, »λάβετε παιδείαν«, φησί, »καὶ μὴ ἀργύριον, καὶ γνῶσιν ὑπὲρ χρυσίον δεδοκιμασμένον· κρείσσων γὰρ σοφία λίθων πολυτελῶν, πᾶν δὲ τίμιον οὐκ ἄξιον αὐτῆς ἐστι.« καὶ πάλιν· »ἐμὲ καρπίζεσθαι ὑπὲρ χρυσίον καὶ λίθον τίμιον καὶ ἄργυρον· τὰ γὰρ ἐμὰ γενήματα κρείττω ἀργυρίου ἐκλεκτοῦ.« εἰ δὲ καὶ διελεῖν χρή, πλούσιος μὲν ὁ πολυκτήμων ἔστω, χρυσίῳ σεσαγμένος καθάπερ φασκώλιον ἐρρυπωμένον, εὐσχήμων δὲ ὁ δίκαιος, ἐπεὶ εὐσχημοσύνη τάξις ἐστὶν ἐν τῷ δέοντι σχηματισμῷ περὶ τὰς διοικήσεις καὶ τὰς ἐπιδόσεις μεμετρημένη· »εἰσὶ γὰρ οἱ σπείροντες καὶ πλείονα συνάγοντες«, περὶ ὧν γέγραπται· »ἐσκόρπισεν, ἔδωκεν τοῖς πένησιν, ἡ δικαιοσύνη αὐτοῦ μένει εἰς τὸν αἰῶνα.« ὥστε οὐχ ὁ ἔχων καὶ φυλάττων, ἀλλ᾿ ὁ μεταδιδοὺς πλούσιος, καὶ ἡ μετάδοσις τὸν μακάριον, οὐχ ἡ κτῆσις δείκνυσι· καρπὸς δὲ ψυχῆς τὸ εὐμετάδοτον· ἐν ψυχῇ ἄρα τὸ πλούσιον. καὶ μὴν τὰ μὲν ἀγαθὰ ἔστω μόνοις κτητὰ τοῖς ἀγαθοῖς, ἀγαθοὶ δὲ οἱ Χριστιανοί· ἄφρων δὲ ἢ ἀκόλαστος ἄνθρωπος οὔτ᾿ ἂν αἴσθησιν ἀγαθοῦ σχοίη οὔτ᾿ ἄν κτήσεως τύχοι· μόνοις ἄρα τοῖς Χριστιανοῖς κτητὰ τὰ ἀγαθά. τούτων δὲ τῶν ἀγαθῶν πλουσιώτερον οὐθέν· πλούσιοι ἄρα οὗτοι μόνοι. πλοῦτος γὰρ ἀληθινὸς ἡ δικαιοσύνη καὶ ὁ παντὸς θησαυροῦ πολυτιμότερος λόγος οὐκ ἀπὸ θρεμμάτων καὶ χωρίων αὐξανόμενος, ἀλλ᾿ ὑπὸ τοῦ θεοῦ δωρούμενος, πλοῦτος ἀναφαίρετος (ἡ ψυχὴ μόνη θησαυρὸς αὐτοῦ), κτῆμα τῷ κεκτημένῳ ἄριστον, μακάριον τῇ ἀληθείᾳ παρεχόμενον τὸν ἄνθρωπον. ᾧ γὰρ ἂν ὑπάρχῃ μηδενὸς μὲν ὀρέγεσθαι τῶν οὐκ ἐφ᾿ ἡμῖν, ὧν δὲ ὀρέγεται, τούτων τυγχάνειν, ἀλλὰ καὶ ὧν ὁσίως ἐφίεται, ταῦτα αἰτούμενον λαμβάνειν παρὰ θεοῦ, πῶς οὗτος οὐ πολυκτήμων καὶ παγκτήμων, θησαυρὸν ἔχων αἰώνιον τὸν θεόν; »τῷ αἰτοῦντι«, φησί, »δοθήσεται καὶ τῷ κρούοντι ἀνοιγήσεται.« εἰ μηδὲν ἀρνεῖται ὁ θεός, τὰ πάντα τοῦ θεοσεβοῦς γίνεται.
pass_a_gloss: Therefore, wealth must be received in a worthy manner and given out in a loving manner to humanity, not in a boastful or arrogant way, and the love of beauty must not be turned into self-love and ignorance, lest someone say to us: his horse is worth fifteen talents or his estate or his servant or his gold, but he himself is worth only three coppers. Immediately, then, consider the world of women and the servants of masters, and you will find them not differing from silver coins. The masters, not in their gait, not in their glance, not in their speech; thus they resemble their slaves. But also, they are distinguished by being weaker than their servants and by being more sickly. It is best, therefore, to sing this doctrine in every circumstance, that the good man, being prudent and just, stores up his wealth in heaven; this man, having sold his earthly possessions and given to the poor, finds the imperishable treasure, where there is no moth, no thief; this man is truly blessed, whether he is small, weak, and insignificant, and he truly possesses the greatest wealth. But if someone is rich like Cinuras and Midas, yet is unjust and arrogant, like the one who revels in purple and fine linen and despises Lazarus, he is wretched and lives a miserable life and will not live. It seems to me that wealth is like a reptile, which, if someone does not know how to handle it safely, will twist around his hand and bite; and wealth is also dangerous, slipping away from the experienced or inexperienced handling, and bites, unless someone uses it with great wisdom, so that, with the help of the word, he may tame the beast, and himself remain unharmed. But, as it seems, the rich man, having acquired the most valuable things, is alone in his ignorance; the most valuable things are not stone, not silver, not clothing, not bodily beauty, but virtue, which is the word given through the pedagogue for practice; this word, which renounces luxury, calls upon self-sufficiency as a servant, and praises the simplicity of prudence, saying, 'Receive education, and not silver, and knowledge, which is more valuable than gold.' And again: 'I am more valuable than gold and precious stone and silver; for my fruits are more valuable than chosen silver.' If, then, we must distinguish, let the rich man be the one who has many possessions, loaded with gold like a purse filled with coins, but let the just man be the one who is dignified, since dignity is order in the necessary arrangement of management and distribution; 'for there are those who sow and reap more.' It is written about them: 'He scattered, he gave to the poor, his justice remains forever.' So, it is not the one who has and keeps, but the one who gives, who is rich, and it is giving, not possession, that shows the blessed person; the fruit of the soul is generosity; therefore, true wealth is in the soul. And indeed, the good things are possessed only by the good; the Christians are good; a foolish or unrestrained person neither perceives what is good nor possesses it; therefore, only the Christians possess the good things. And of these good things, there is nothing more valuable; therefore, these people are the only rich ones. For true wealth is justice and the word, which is more valuable than all treasure, not increasing from cattle and estates, but given by God, wealth that cannot be taken away, the soul being its only treasure, the best possession for the one who possesses it, making the person blessed with truth. For the one who has nothing to desire of the things that are not in his power, and of the things he desires, he obtains, and also, the things he rightly asks for, he receives from God, how is this person not rich in many things and all things, having the eternal treasure, God? 'To the one who asks,' it is said, 'it will be given, and to the one who knocks, it will be opened.' If God does not deny anything, all things become the things of the one who reveres God.

lemmas.gloss: in a loving manner to humanity

pass_b_english: Wealth, therefore, must be accepted in a worthy manner and shared generously, not in a mercenary or boastful spirit. We must not let the love of beauty turn into self-love and ignorance, or someone may say of us: his horse is worth fifteen talents, or his estate, or his servant, or his gold, yet he himself is valued at only three copper coins. Look at once at the world of women and the servants of masters; you will find them indistinguishable from purchased silver. Their masters — not in their walk, not in their glance, not in their speech — so closely resemble their slaves. They are even distinguished by being weaker than their servants and by having been reared more sickly. This doctrine, then, is best to sing in every circumstance: the good man, being prudent and just, stores up his wealth in heaven. By selling his earthly possessions and giving to the poor, he finds the imperishable treasure where no moth destroys and no thief breaks in (Matt 6:19-20). He is truly blessed, even if he is small, weak, and insignificant, and he truly possesses the greatest wealth. But if someone is richer than Cinuras and Midas, yet is unjust and arrogant — like the man who revels in purple and fine linen and despises Lazarus (Luke 16:19-21) — he is wretched, lives miserably, and will not live. To me, wealth seems like a reptile: if a person does not know how to handle it safely, it will coil around his hand and bite from the harmless tip of its tail. Wealth is also dangerous when it slips away, whether from experienced or inexperienced handling, and bites, unless someone uses it with superior wisdom so that, with the incantation of the Word, he may tame the beast and himself remain unharmed. Yet, as it appears, the rich man who has acquired the most valuable things is alone in his ignorance. The most valuable things are not stone, not silver, not clothing, not bodily beauty, but virtue — which is the Word handed down through the Paedagogus for training. This Word renounces luxury, calls self-sufficiency as its servant, and praises the frugality born of prudence, saying, "Receive instruction, and not silver, and knowledge rather than choice gold" (Prov 8:10). And again: "I am more valuable than gold and precious stone and silver; for my fruits are better than choice silver" (Prov 8:19). If we must distinguish, let the rich man be the one with many possessions, burdened with gold like a soiled money-bag, but let the just man be the dignified one, since dignity is order in the proper arrangement of management and measured distribution. "For there are those who sow and reap more," concerning whom it is written: "He scattered abroad, he gave to the poor; his righteousness endures forever" (Ps 112:9; 2 Cor 9:9). So it is not the one who has and keeps, but the one who shares, who is rich; and it is giving, not possession, that shows the blessed person. The fruit of the soul is generosity; therefore true wealth resides in the soul. Indeed, good things belong only to the good, and the good are the Christians. A foolish or unrestrained person neither perceives what is good nor can possess it; therefore only Christians possess good things. Nothing is more valuable than these good things; therefore these alone are the rich. For true wealth is righteousness and the Word, more precious than all treasure — not increasing from flocks and fields, but given by God. It is inalienable wealth (the soul is its only treasury), the best possession for the one who has it, making a person blessed in truth. For whoever desires nothing that is not in his power, obtains what he does desire, and also receives from God whatever he asks for rightly — how is this person not rich in many things and all things, possessing the eternal treasure, God? "To the one who asks, it will be given, and to the one who knocks, it will be opened" (Matt 7:7-8). If God denies nothing, all things become the possession of the God-revering person.

review.notes: The translation accurately captures the nuances of the Greek text. Pass A provides a literal rendering, while Pass B provides a more fluent version with necessary scripture citations (Matt 6:19-20, Luke 16:19-21, Prov 8:10, Prov 8:19, Ps 112:9, 2 Cor 9:9, Matt 7:7-8) which are required for patristic clarity. The translation of 'ἀκρᾶς οὐρᾶς ἀνακρημνὰς τὸ θηρίον' as 'from the harmless tip of its tail' in Pass B is a valid interpretive rendering of the imagery. All clauses, including the complex description of the reptile and the distinction between the rich man and the just man, are preserved.
